claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition.
The magnetostructural transition is first order.
Changing deposition temperature can produce a refined, nanocrystalline microstructure with greater grain-boundary density.
Changing deposition rate is equivalent to changing deposition temperature for inducing the proposed microstructural refinement.
Grain-size reduction and increased interfacial area modify the magnetostructural-transition dynamics.
Numerous interfaces enhance nucleation of the magnetostructural transition.
Interface-enhanced nucleation lowers the energy barrier for the magnetostructural transition.
Microstructural refinement alleviates interface pinning and thereby reduces transition abruptness and hysteresis.
A refined microstructure will produce a broader and smoother magnetocaloric response.
Nanocrystalline refinement will reduce coercivity relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Nanocrystalline refinement will reduce hysteretic energy loss relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The refined samples will have a broader magnetocaloric peak and reduced transition sharpness.
Microstructural refinement will improve heat-exchange performance.
The baseline has limited heat-exchange rates because of its coarse microstructure.
Coercivity can be affected by grain size and other microstructural features.
The predictions apply only when refinement occurs without secondary-phase formation or loss of mechanical stability.
The predictions are restricted to low-applied-field magnetic-cooling operation.

contradictions.description: The initial state and intervention describe an as-deposited thin-film system, whereas the baseline calls the original as-deposited alloy an arc-melted or melt-spun material. Arc-melted ingots are not an as-deposited thin-film baseline, so the physical form and preparation route of the control are inconsistent.

The boundary excludes samples in which secondary phases form, but the falsification rule treats secondary-phase formation as falsifying the mechanism. Such formation instead places the sample outside the stated prediction domain and does not directly test the proposed grain-boundary mechanism.
